entries.06694d2774e34ffddf19861cfd81aecec51efe38: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9559"/><div sID="gen16746" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9559"/><hi type="bold">11. suck--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.60.5">Is 60:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.60.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.6">61:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.23">49:23</reference>).<div eID="gen16746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abundance--</hi>Hebrew, "the ray-like flow of her opulence," that is, with the milk spouting out from her full breasts (answering to the parallel, "breast of her consolations") in ray-like streams [Gesenius]. <div eID="gen16747" type="x-p"/>
entries.d0c07d16522518d5defe59e981b131068456ff11: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9560"/><div sID="gen16748" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9560"/><hi type="bold">12. extend--</hi>I will turn peace (prosperity) upon her, like a river turned in its course [Gesenius]. Or, "I will spread peace over her as an overflowing river" [Barnes], (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.18">Is 48:18</reference>).<div eID="gen16748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16749" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flowing stream--</hi>as the Nile by its overflow fertilizes the whole of Egypt.<div eID="gen16749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16750" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">borne upon ... sides--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.60.4">Is 60:4</reference>).<div eID="gen16750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16751" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">her ... her--</hi>If "ye" refers to the Jews, translate, "ye shall be borne upon their sides ... their knees," namely, those of the Gentiles, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.49.22">Is 49:22</reference>; and as "suck" (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.16">Is 60:16</reference>) refers to the Jews sucking the Gentile wealth. However, English Version gives a good sense: The Jews, and all who love Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.10">Is 66:10</reference>), "shall suck, and be borne" by her as a mother. <div eID="gen16751" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b66061286ea7488ced32a633db3da247e7c1cc5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9561"/><div sID="gen16752" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9561"/><hi type="bold">13. mother--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.49.15">Is 49:15</reference>).<div eID="gen16752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16753" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">comforteth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.40.1">Is 40:1</reference>, 2). <div eID="gen16753" type="x-p"/>

entries.ec048ce0dc4c3cbc0c5efacfb00551025f57b3bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9563"/><div sID="gen16757" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9563"/>15. entries.d0ef9b6a31bcd5c57d9d195d1f5e85f372ea34e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9564"/><div sID="gen16761" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9564"/>16. entries.272d28d5bf2ddf5bb95dac528f6be97359a2f03d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9565"/><div sID="gen16763" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9565"/><hi type="bold">17. in ... gardens--</hi>Hebrew and the Septuagint rather require, "for (entering into) gardens," namely, to sacrifice there [Maurer].<div eID="gen16763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16764" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">behind one tree--</hi>rather, "following one," that is, some idol or other, which, from contempt, he does not name [Maurer]. Vitringa, &c., think the Hebrew for "one," Ahhadh, to be the name of the god; called Adad (meaning One) in Syria (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.17.23">Ac 17:23</reference>). The idol's power was represented by inclined rays, as of the sun shining on the earth. Gesenius translates, "following one," namely, Hierophant ("priest"), who led the rest in performing the sacred rites.<div eID="gen16764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in ... midst--</hi>namely, of the garden (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.65.3">Is 65:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.4">4</reference>).<div eID="gen16765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16766" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mouse--</hi>legally unclean (<reference osisRef="Lev.11.29">Le 11:29</reference>) because it was an idol to the heathen (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.37.36">Is 37:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.4">1Sa 6:4</reference>). Translate, "the field mouse," or "dormouse" [Bochart]. The Pharisees with their self-righteous purifications, and all mere formalists, are included in the same condemnation, described in language taken from the idolatries prevalent in Isaiah's times. <div eID="gen16766" type="x-p"/>
entries.f0dff9ad588a8e91c2fc1a842f6eadeff0d43075: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9566"/><div sID="gen16767" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9566"/><hi type="bold">18. know--</hi>not in the Hebrew. [Maurer].<div eID="gen16768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gather ... nations--</hi>against Jerusalem, where the ungodly Jews shall perish; and then the Lord at last shall fight for Jerusalem against those nations: and the survivors (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.19">Is 66:19</reference>) shall "see God's glory" (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.8">Zec 12:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.12.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.1-Zech.14.3">14:1-3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.9">9</reference>).<div eID="gen16769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16770" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tongues--</hi>which have been many owing to sin, being confounded at Babel, but which shall again be one in Christ (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">Da 7:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.9">Zep 3:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Re 7:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen16770" type="x-p"/>
entries.f31deb8b41e343bfc1743e7a327d79a6b34b642f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9567"/><div sID="gen16771" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9567"/><hi type="bold">19. sign--</hi>a banner on a high place, to indicate the place of meeting for the dispersed Jewish exiles, preparatory to their return to their land (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.26">Is 5:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.12">11:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.10">62:10</reference>).<div eID="gen16771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16772" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">those that escape of them--</hi>the Gentile survivors spared by God (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.66.18">Is 66:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.16">Zec 14:16</reference>). <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Is 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.7">Mi 5:7</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Zech.14.16-Zech.14.19">Zec 14:16-19</reference> represent it, not that the Jews go as missionaries to the Gentiles, but that the Gentiles come up to Jerusalem to learn the Lord's ways there.<div eID="gen16772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16773" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Tarshish--</hi>Tartessus in Spain, in the west.<div eID="gen16773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16774" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Pul--</hi>east and north of Africa: probably the same as Philoe, an island in the Nile, called by the Egyptians Pilak, that is, the border country, being between Egypt and Ethiopia [Bochart].<div eID="gen16774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16775" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lud--</hi>the Libyans of Africa (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.13">Ge 10:13</reference>), Ludim being son of Mizraim (Egypt): an Ethiopian people famous as bowmen (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.9">Jr 46:9</reference>): employed as mercenaries by Tyre and Egypt (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.10">Eze 27:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.5">30:5</reference>).<div eID="gen16775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16776" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Tubal--</hi>Tibarenians, in Asia Minor, south of the Caucasus, between the Black Sea and Araxes. Or, the Iberians [Josephus]. Italy [Jerome].<div eID="gen16776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16777" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Javan--</hi>the Greeks; called Ionians, including all the descendants of Javan, both in Greece and in Asia Minor (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.2-Gen.10.4">Ge 10:2-4</reference>).<div eID="gen16777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16778" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my glory ... Gentiles--</hi>(Mal 1:11). <div eID="gen16778" type="x-p"/>
entries.bad027a193545152ff90a38dec4b1c5045f7ea21: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9568"/><div sID="gen16779" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9568"/><hi type="bold">20. they--</hi>the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.19">Is 66:19</reference>).<div eID="gen16779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16780" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring ... your brethren--</hi>the Jews, back to the Holy Land (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.22">Is 49:22</reference>). It cannot mean the mere entrance of the Jews into the Christian Church; for such an entrance would be by faith, not upon "horses, litters, and mules" [Houbigant]. "Offering" is metaphorical, as in <reference osisRef="Rom.15.16">Ro 15:16</reference>.<div eID="gen16780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16781" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">horses--</hi>not much used by the Jews. The Gentiles are here represented as using their modes of conveyance to "bring" the Jews to Jerusalem.<div eID="gen16781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16782" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chariots--</hi>as these are not found in Oriental caravans, translate, "vehicles," namely, borne, not drawn on wheels.<div eID="gen16782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16783" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">litters--</hi>covered sedans for the rich.<div eID="gen16783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16784" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon swift beasts--</hi>dromedaries: from Hebrew root, "to dance," from their bounding motion, often accelerated by music [Bochart]. Panniers were thrown across the dromedaries' back for poorer women [Horsley]. <div eID="gen16784" type="x-p"/>

entries.5d36cdff675505b8a325c678e6f3eafea1409d1f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9571"/><div sID="gen16788" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9571"/>23. Literally, "As often as the new moon (shall be) in its own new moon," that is, every month (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.16">Zec 14:16</reference>).<div eID="gen16788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16789" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sabbath--</hi>which is therefore perpetually obligatory on earth.<div eID="gen16789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16790" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all flesh--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.65.2">Psa 65:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.11">72:11</reference>).<div eID="gen16790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16791" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before me--</hi>at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.16">Jr 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">17</reference>). <div eID="gen16791" type="x-p"/>
entries.e6a3871048db0da46189736da63cde0871301f72: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9572"/><div sID="gen16792" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9572"/><hi type="bold">24. go forth, and look--</hi>as the Israelites looked at the carcasses of the Egyptians destroyed at the Red Sea (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.30">Ex 14:30</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.26.14-Isa.26.19">Is 26:14-19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.58.10">Psa 58:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">49:14</reference>; Mal 4:1-3).<div eID="gen16792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16793" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">carcasses, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.66.16">Is 66:16</reference>), those slain by the Lord in the last great battle near Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.2-Zech.9.14">Zec 12:2-9; 14</reference>:2-4); type of the final destruction of all sinners.<div eID="gen16793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16794" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">worm ... not die--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Mark.9.44">Mr 9:44</reference>, 46, 48). Image of hell, from bodies left unburied in the valley of Hinnom (whence comes Gehenna, or "hell"), south of Jerusalem, where a perpetual fire was kept to consume the refuse thrown there (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Is 30:33</reference>). It shall not be inconsistent with true love for the godly to look with satisfaction on God's vengeance on the wicked (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.10">Re 14:10</reference>). May God bless this Commentary, and especially its solemn close, to His glory, and to the edification of the writer and the readers of it, for Jesus' sake! <chapter eID="Isa.66"/><div eID="gen16794" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen13185" osisID="Isa" type="book"/>

entries.1833cfd7871c85dd12bf1759fe143b0b604477ef: <div eID="gen29087" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29088" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29089" type="x-p"/> This chapter treats of the same subject with the foregoing. God, by his prophet, tells the Jews, who valued themselves much on their temple and pompous worship, that the Most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands; and that no outward rites of worship, while the worshippers are idolatrous and impure, can please him who looketh at the heart, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.1-Isa.66.3">Isa 66:1-3</reference>. This leads to a threatening of vengeance for their guilt, alluding to their making void the law of God by their abominable traditions, their rejection of Christ, persecution of his followers, and consequent destruction by the Romans. But as the Jewish ritual and people shadow forth the system of Christianity and its professors; so, in the prophetical writings, the idolatries of the Jews are frequently put for the idolatries afterwards practiced by those bearing the Christian name. Consequently, if we would have the plenitude of meaning in this section of prophecy, which the very content requires, we must look through the type into the antitype, viz., the very gross idolatries practiced by the members of Antichrist, the pompous heap of human intentions and traditions with which they have encumbered the Christian system, their most dreadful persecution of Christ's spiritual and true worshippers, and the awful judgments which shall overtake them in the great and terrible day of the Lord, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.4-Isa.66.6">Isa 66:4-6</reference>. The mighty and sudden increase of the Church of Jesus Christ at the period of Antichrist's fall represented by the very strong figure of Sion being delivered of a man-child before the time of her travail, the meaning of which symbol the prophet immediately subjoins in a series of interrogations for the sake of greater force and emphasis, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.7-Isa.66.9">Isa 66:7-9</reference>. Wonderful prosperity and unspeakable blessedness of the world when the posterity of Jacob, with the fullness of the Gentiles, shall be assembled to Messiah's standard, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.10-Isa.66.14">Isa 66:10-14</reference>. All the wicked of the earth shall be gathered together to the battle of that great day of God Almighty, and the slain of Jehovah shall be many, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.15-Isa.66.18">Isa 66:15-18</reference>. Manner of the future restoration of the Israelites from their several dispersions throughout the habitable globe, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.19-Isa.66.21">Isa 66:19-21</reference>. Perpetuity of this new economy of grace to the house of Israel, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.22">Isa 66:22</reference>. Righteousness shall be universally diffused in the earth; and the memory of those who have transgressed against the Lord shall be had in continual abhorrence, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.23">Isa 66:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.24">Isa 66:24</reference>. Thus this great prophet, after tracing the principal events of time, seems at length to have terminated his views in eternity, where all revolutions cease, where the blessedness of the righteous shall be unchangeable as the new heavens, and the misery of the wicked as the fire that shall not be quenched. <div eID="gen29089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29090" type="x-p"/> This chapter is a continuation of the subject of the foregoing. The Jews valued themselves much upon their temple, and the pompous system of services performed in it, which they supposed were to be of perpetual duration; and they assumed great confidence and merit to themselves for their strict observance of all the externals of their religion. And at the very time when the judgments denounced in <reference osisRef="Isa.65.6">Isa 65:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.65.12">Isa 65:12</reference> of the preceding chapter were hanging over their heads, they were rebuilding, by Herod's munificence, the temple in a most magnificent manner. God admonishes them, that "the Most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands;" and that a mere external worship, how diligently soever attended, when accompanied with wicked and idolatrous practices in the worshippers, would never be accepted by him. This their hypocrisy is set forth in strong colors, which brings the prophet again to the subject of the former chapter; and he pursues it in a different manner, with more express declaration of the new economy, and of the flourishing state of the Church under it. The increase of the Church is to be sudden and astonishing. They that escape of the Jews, that is, that become converts to the Christian faith, are to be employed in the Divine mission to the Gentiles, and are to act as priests in presenting the Gentiles as an offering to God; see <reference osisRef="Rom.15.16">Rom 15:16</reference>. And both, now collected into one body, shall be witnesses of the final perdition of the obstinate and irreclaimable. <div eID="gen29090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29091" type="x-p"/> These two chapters manifestly relate to the calling of the Gentiles, the establishment of the Christian dispensation, and the reprobation of the apostate Jews, and their destruction executed by the Romans. - L.
entries.718be09cc4c6067a28ae16e11b7e8167eef13edf: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen29091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29092" type="x-p"/> And all those things have been "And all these things are mine" - A word absolutely necessary to the sense is here lost out of the text: לי li, mine. It is preserved by the Septuagint and Syriac.
entries.78ffb77c313c4bb53b8afc01f3cde41448ae816f: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen29092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29093" type="x-p"/> He that killeth an ox is as if he slew a man "He that slayeth an ox killeth a man" - These are instances of wickedness joined with hypocrisy; of the most flagitious crimes committed by those who at the same time affected great strictness in the performance of all the external services of religion. God, by the Prophet Ezekiel, upbraids the Jews with the same practices: "When they had slain their children to their idols, then they came the same day into my sanctuary to profane it," <reference osisRef="Eze.23.39">Eze 23:39</reference>. Of the same kind was the hypocrisy of the Pharisees in our Savior's time:" who devoured widows' houses, and for a pretense made long prayers," <reference osisRef="Mat.23.14">Mat 23:14</reference>. <div eID="gen29093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29094" type="x-p"/> The generality of interpreters, by departing from the literal rendering of the text, have totally lost the true sense of it, and have substituted in its place what makes no good sense at all; for it is not easy to show how, in any circumstances, sacrifice and murder, the presenting of legal offerings and idolatrous worship, can possibly be of the same account in the sight of God. <div eID="gen29094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29095" type="x-p"/> He that offereth an oblation, as if he offered swine's blood "That maketh an oblation offereth swine's blood" - A word here likewise, necessary to complete the sense, is perhaps irrecoverably lost out of the text. The Vulgate and Chaldee add the word offereth, to make out the sense; not, as I imagine, from any different reading, (for the word wanted seems to have been lost before the time of the oldest of them as the Septuagint had it not in their copy,; but from mere necessity. <div eID="gen29095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29096" type="x-p"/> Le Clerc thinks that מעלה maaleh is to be repeated from the beginning of this member; but that is not the case in the parallel members, which have another and a different verb in the second place, "דם dam, sic Versiones; putarem tamen legendum participium aliquod, et quidem זבח zabach, cum sequatur ח cheth, nisi jam praecesserat." - Secker. Houbigant supplies אכל achal, eateth. After all, I think the most probable word is that which the Chaldee and Vulgate seem to have designed to represent; that is, מקריב makrib, offereth. <div eID="gen29096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29097" type="x-p"/> In their abominations - ובשקוציהם ubeshikkutseyhem, "and in their abominations;" two copies of the Machazor, and one of Kennicott's MSS. have ובגלוליהם ubegilluleyhem, "and in their idols." So the Vulgate and Syriac.
entries.77c246795b66dcdcd7adde6620b0d512acb1000b: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen29097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29098" type="x-p"/> Your brethren that hated you - said "Say ye to your brethren that hate you" - The Syriac reads אמרו לאחיכם imru laacheychem; and so the Septuagint, Edit. Comp. ειπατε αδελφοις ὑμων· and MS. Marchal. has αδελφοις· and so Cyril and Procopius read and explain it. It is not easy to make sense of the reading of the Septuagint in the other editions; ειπατε αδελφοι ἡμων τοις μισουσιν ὑμας· but for ἡμων, our, MS. 1. D. 2 also has ὑμων, your.
entries.ebabdf700c3c3065c511e9f3cbdfe9a804c9eb2b: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen29098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29099" type="x-p"/> A voice of noise from the city, a voice from the temple, a voice of the Lord - It is very remarkable that similar words were spoken by Jesus, son of Ananias, previously to the destruction of Jerusalem. See his very affecting history related by Josephus, War, B. vi., chap. v.
entries.7ad4baf49b4e4e238f3718b8b05e0c516e9022ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen29099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29100" type="x-p"/> Who hath seen "And who hath seen" - Twenty MSS., (four ancient), of Kennicott's, and twenty-nine of De Rossi's, and two ancient of my own, and the two oldest editions, with two others, have ומי umi, adding the conjunction ו vau; and so read all the ancient versions. And who hath seen?
entries.44d8acfff209fe8a2fd2c947388f3c1944cb26f5: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen29100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29101" type="x-p"/> Shall I bring to the birth - האני אשביר haani ashbir, num ego matricem frangam; Montanus. The word means that which immediately precedes the appearance of the fetus - the breaking forth of the liquor amnii. This also is an expression that should be studiously avoided in prayers and sermons.
entries.5a824f455f204e67c706bda1515b4a20df26d6cc: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen29101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29102" type="x-p"/> With the abundance of her glory "From her abundant stores" - For מזיז mizziz, from the splendor, two MSS. and the old edition of 1488, have מזיו mizziv; and the latter ז zain is upon a rasure in three other MSS. It is remarkable that Kimchi and Sal. ben Melec, not being able to make any thing of the word as it stands in the text, say it means the same with מזיו mizziv; that is, in effect, they admit of a various reading, or an error in the text. But as Vitringa observes, what sense is there in sucking nourishment from the splendor of her glory? He therefore endeavors to deduce another sense of the word זיז ziz; but, as far as it appears to me, without any authority. I am more inclined to accede to the opinion of those learned rabbins, and to think that there is some mistake in the word; for that in truth is their opinion, though they disguise it by saying that the corrupted word means the very same with that which they believe to be genuine. So in <reference osisRef="Isa.41.24">Isa 41:24</reference> they say that אפע apha, a viper, means the same with אפס ephes, nothing; instead of acknowledging that one is written by mistake instead of the other. I would propose to read in this place מזין mizzin or מזן mizzen, which is the reading of one of De Rossi's MS., (instead of מזיז meziz), from the stores, from זון zun, to nourish, to feed; see <reference osisRef="Gen.45.23">Gen 45:23</reference>;<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.23">2Chr 11:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.144.13">Psa 144:13</reference>. And this perhaps may be meant by Aquila, who renders the word by απο παντοδαπιας· with which that of the Vulgate, ab omnimoda gloria, and of Symmachus and Theodotion, nearly agree. The Chaldee follows a different reading, without improving the sense; מיין meyin, from the wine. - L.
entries.96c596ae9f0e09246707df2bdca7632aa3a206c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen29102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29103" type="x-p"/> Like a river, and - like a flowing stream "Like the great river, and like the overflowing stream" - That is, the Euphrates, (it ought to have been pointed כנהר cannahar, ut fluvius ille, as the river), and the Nile. <div eID="gen29103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29104" type="x-p"/> Then shall ye suck "And ye shall suck at the breast" - These two words על שד al shad, at the breast, seem to have been omitted in the present text, from their likeness to the two words following; על צד al tsad, at the side. A very probable conjecture of Houbigant. The Chaldee and Vulgate have omitted the two latter words instead of the two former. See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.60.4">Isa 60:4</reference> (note).
entries.34811b14c1f1723b993761965bccf71910d96247: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen29104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29105" type="x-p"/> The Lord will come with fire "Jehovah shall come as a fire" - For באש baesh, in fire, the Septuagint had in their copy קאש kaesh, as a fire; ὡς πυρ. <div eID="gen29105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29106" type="x-p"/> To render his anger with fury "To breathe forth his anger in a burning heat" - Instead of להשב lehashib, as pointed by the Masoretes, to render, I understand it as להשב lehashshib, to breathe, from נשב nashab.
entries.530b4d97ff8e37324d12f601d9e8034c64919cc0: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen29106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29107" type="x-p"/> Behind one tree "After the rites of Achad" - The Syrians worshipped a god called Adad, Plin. Nat. Hist. 37:11; Macrob. Sat. 1:23. They held him to be the highest and greatest of the gods, and to be the same with Jupiter and the sun; and the name Adad, says Macrobius, signifies one; as likewise does the word Achad in Isaiah. Many learned men therefore have supposed, and with some probability, that the prophet means the same pretended deity. אחד achad, in the Syrian and Chaldean dialects, is חד chad; and perhaps by reduplication of the last letter to express perfect unity, it may have become חדד chadad, not improperly expressed by Macrobius Adad, without the aspirate. It was also pronounced by the Syrians themselves, with a weaker aspirate, הדד hadad, as in Benhadad, Hadadezer, names of their kings, which were certainly taken from their chief object of worship. This seems to me to be a probable account of this name. <div eID="gen29107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29108" type="x-p"/> But the Masoretes correct the text in this place. Their marginal reading is אחת achath which is the same word, only in the feminine form; and so read thirty MSS. (six ancient) and the two oldest editions. This Le Clerc approves, and supposes it to mean Hecate, or the moon; and he supports his hypothesis by arguments not at all improbable. See his note on the place. <div eID="gen29108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29109" type="x-p"/> Whatever the particular mode of idolatry which the prophet refers to might be, the general sense of the place is perfectly clear. But the Chaldee and Syriac, and after them Symmachus and Theodotion, cut off at once all these difficulties, by taking the word אחד achad in its common meaning, not as a proper name; the two latter rendering the sentence thus: Οπισω αλληλων εν μεσῳ εσθιοντων το κρεας το χοιρειον; "One after another, in the midst of those that eat swine's flesh." I suppose they all read in their copies אחד אחד achad achad, one by one, or perhaps אחד אחר אחד achad achar achad, one after another. See a large dissertation on this subject in Davidis Millii Dissertationes Selectae, Dissert. vi. - L. <div eID="gen29109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29110" type="x-p"/> I know not what to make of this place; it is certain that our translation makes no sense, and that of the learned prelate seems to me too refined. Kimchi interprets this of the Turks, who are remarkable for ablutions. "Behind one in the midst" he understands of a large fish-pond placed in the middle of their gardens. Others make אחד achad a deity, as above; and a deity of various names it is supposed to be, for it is Achad, and Chad, and Hadad, and Achath, and Hecat, an Assyrian idol. Behynd the fyrst tree or the gate withine forth. - Old MS. Bible.
entries.4552d12a721e8694ac1c0fc77b814a6f07bba3f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen29110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29111" type="x-p"/> For I know their works - A word is here lost out of the present text, leaving the text quite imperfect. The word is יודע yodea, knowing, supplied from the Syriac. The Chaldee had the same word in the copy before him, which he paraphrases by קדמי גלן kedemi gelon, their deeds are manifest before me; and the Aldine and Complutensian editions of the Septuagint acknowledge the same word επισταμαι, which is verified by MS. Pachom. and the Arabic version. I think there can be little doubt of its being genuine. The concluding verses of this chapter refer to the complete restoration of the Jews, and to the destruction of all the enemies of the Gospel of Christ, so that the earth shall be filled with the knowledge and glory of the Lord. Talia saecla currite! Lord, hasten the time! <div eID="gen29111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29112" type="x-p"/> It shall come "And I come" - For באה baah, which will not accord with any thing in the sentence, I read בא ba, with a MS.; the participle answering to יודע yodea, with which agree the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate. Perhaps it ought to be ובא veba, when I shall come, Syr.; and so the Septuagint, according to Edit. Ald. and Complut., and Cod. Marchal.
entries.159e4b2d26a83348da4588e3e8a44966adf1679f: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen29112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29113" type="x-p"/> That draw the bow - I much suspect that the words משכי קשת moshechey kesheth, who draw the bow, are a corruption of the word משך meshek, Moschi, the name of a nation situated between the Euxine and Caspian seas; and properly joined with תבל tubal, the Tibareni. See Bochart, Phaleg. <reference osisRef="Isa.3.12">Isa 3:12</reference>. The Septuagint have μοσοχ, without any thing of the drawers of the bow: the word being once taken for a participle, the bow was added to make sense of it קשת kesheth, the bow, is omitted in a MS. and by the Septuagint. <div eID="gen29113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29114" type="x-p"/> That have not heard my fame "Who never heard my name" - For שמעי shimi, my fame, I read, with the Septuagint and Syriac, שמי shemi, my name.
entries.e9973e97dffc2ccfe1b65ee095e945125683a194: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen29114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29115" type="x-p"/> And in chariots "And in counes" - There is a sort of vehicle much used in the east, consisting of a pair of hampers or cradles, thrown across a camel's back, one on each side; in each of which a person is carried. They have a covering to defend them from the rain and the sun. Thevenot calls them counes, 1 p. 356. Maillet describes them as covered cages hanging on both sides of a camel. "At Aleppo," says Dr. Russell, "women of inferior condition in longer journeys are commonly stowed, one on each side of a mule, in a sort of covered cradles." Nat. Hist. of Aleppo, p. 89. These seem to be what the prophet means by the word צבים tsabbim. Harmer's Observations, 1 p. 445.
entries.27c41beca8cb7cfe1ce27ba186f5757e1ef896ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen29115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29116" type="x-p"/> And for Levites - For ללוים laleviyim, fifty-nine MSS., (eight ancient), have וללוים velaleviyim, adding the conjunction ו vau, which the sense seems necessarily to require: and so read all the ancient versions. See <reference osisRef="Jos.3.3">Jos 3:3</reference>, and the various readings on that place in Kennicott's Bible.
entries.176a470d76df9481e43cedffd94ffdc4c58a9399: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen29116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29117" type="x-p"/> For their worm shall not die - These words of the prophet are applied by our blessed Savior, <reference osisRef="Mar.9.44">Mar 9:44</reference>, to express the everlasting punishment of the wicked in Gehenna, or in hell. Gehenna, or the valley of Hinnom, was very near to Jerusalem to the south-east: it was the place where the idolatrous Jews celebrated that horrible rite of making their children pass through the fire, that is, of burning them in sacrifice to Moloch. To put a stop to this abominable practice, Josiah defiled, or desecrated, the place, by filling it with human bones, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.10">2Kgs 23:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.14">2Kgs 23:14</reference>; and probably it was the custom afterwards to throw out the carcasses of animals there, when it also became the common burying place for the poorer people of Jerusalem. Our Savior expressed the state of the blessed by sensible images; such as paradise, Abraham's bosom, or, which is the same thing, a place to recline next to Abraham at table in the kingdom of heaven. See <reference osisRef="Mat.8.11">Mat 8:11</reference>. Coenabat Nerva cum paucis. Veiento proxies, atque etiam in sinu recumbebat. "The Emperor Nerva supped with few. Veiento was the first in his estimation, and even reclined in his bosom." Plin. Epist. 4:22. Compare <reference osisRef="Joh.13.23">Joh 13:23</reference>; for we could not possibly have any conception of it but by analogy from worldly objects. In like manner he expressed the place of torment under the image of Gehenna; and the punishment of the wicked by the worm which there preyed on the carcasses, and the fire that consumed the wretched victims. Marking however, in the strongest manner, the difference between Gehenna and the invisible place of torment; namely, that in the former the suffering is transient: - the worm itself which preys upon the body, dies; and the fire which totally consumes it, is soon extinguished: - whereas in the figurative Gehenna the instruments of punishment shall be everlasting, and the suffering without end; "for there the worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched." <div eID="gen29117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29118" type="x-p"/> These emblematical images, expressing heaven and hell, were in use among the Jews before our Savior's time; and in using them he complied with their notions. "Blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God," says the Jew to our Savior, <reference osisRef="Luk.14.15">Luk 14:15</reference>. And in regard to Gehenna, the Chaldee paraphrase as I observed before on <reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Isa 30:33</reference>, renders everlasting or continual burnings by "the Gehenna of everlasting fire." And before his time the son of Sirach, 7:17, had said, "The vengeance of the ungodly is fire and worms." So likewise the author of the book of Judith, chap. 16:17: "Wo to the nations rising up against my kindred: the Lord Almighty will take vengeance of them in the day of judgment, in putting fire and worms in their flesh;" manifestly referring to the same emblem. - L. <div eID="gen29118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29119" type="x-p"/> Kimchi's conclusion of his notes on this book is remarkable: - "Blessed be God who hath created the mountains and the hills, <div eID="gen29119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29120" type="x-p"/> And hath endued me with strength to finish the book of salvation: <div eID="gen29120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29121" type="x-p"/> He shall rejoice us with good tidings and reports; <div eID="gen29121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29122" type="x-p"/> He shall show us a token for good: - <div eID="gen29122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29123" type="x-p"/> And the end of his miracles he shall cause to approach us." <div eID="gen29123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29124" type="x-p"/> Several of the Versions have a peculiarity in their terminations: - <div eID="gen29124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29125" type="x-p"/> And they shall be to a satiety of sight to all flesh. <div eID="gen29125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29126" type="x-p"/> Vulgate. <div eID="gen29126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29127" type="x-p"/> And thei schul ben into fyllyng of sigt to all fleshe. <div eID="gen29127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29128" type="x-p"/> Old MS. Bible. <div eID="gen29128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29129" type="x-p"/> And they shall be as a vision to all flesh. <div eID="gen29129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29130" type="x-p"/> Septuagint. <div eID="gen29130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29131" type="x-p"/> And the wicked shall be punished in hell till the righteous shall say, - It is enough. <div eID="gen29131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29132" type="x-p"/> Chaldee. <div eID="gen29132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29133" type="x-p"/> They shall be an astonishment to all flesh; So that they shall be a spectacle to all beings. <div eID="gen29133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29134" type="x-p"/> Syriac. <div eID="gen29134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29135" type="x-p"/> The end of the prophecy of Isaiah the prophet. <div eID="gen29135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29136" type="x-p"/> Praise to God who is truly praiseworthy. <div eID="gen29136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29137" type="x-p"/> Arabic. <div eID="gen29137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29138" type="x-p"/> One of my old Hebrew MSS. after the twenty-first verse repeats the twenty-third: "And it shall come to pass that from one new moon to another, and from one Sabbath to another, shall all flesh come to worship before me, saith the Lord."  <chapter eID="Isa.66"/> <div eID="gen29138" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen26170" osisID="Isa" type="book"/>

entries.f1a301e67499a3e82c39b6b904d29c522856afc2: <reference osisRef="Isa.66.1-Isa.66.4">Isa 66:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen13692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13693" type="x-p"/> Although the note on which this prophecy opens is a different one from any that has yet been struck, there are many points in which it coincides with the preceding prophecy. For not only is <reference osisRef="Isa.65.12">Isa 65:12</reference> repeated here in <reference osisRef="Isa.66.4">Isa 66:4</reference>, but the sharp line of demarcation drawn in chapter 65, between the servants of Jehovah and the worldly majority of the nation with reference to the approaching return to the Holy Land, is continued here. As the idea of their return is associated immediately with that of the erection of a new temple, there is nothing at all to surprise us, after what we have read in Isa 65:8., in the fact that Jehovah expresses His abhorrence at the thought of having a temple built by the Israel of the captivity, as the majority then were, and does so in such words as those which follow in <reference osisRef="Isa.66.1-Isa.66.4">Isa 66:1-4</reference> : <hi type="italic">“Thus saith Jehovah: The heaven is my throne, and the earth my footstool. What kind of house is it that ye would build me, and what kind of place for my rest? My hand hath made all these things; then all these thing arose, saith Jehovah; and at such persons do I look, at the miserable and broken-hearted, and him that trembleth at my word. He that slaughtereth the ox is the slayer of a man; he that sacrificeth the sheep is a strangler of dogs; he that offereth a meat-offering, it is swine’s blood; he that causeth incense to rise up in smoke, blesseth idols. As they have chosen their ways, and their soul cheriseth pleasure in their abominations; so will I choose their ill-treatments, and bring their terrors upon them, because I called and no one replied, I spake and they did not hear, and they did evil in mine eyes, and chose that in which I took no pleasure." </hi> Hitzig is of opinion that the author has broken off here, and proceeds quite unexpectedly to denounce the intention to build a temple for Jehovah. Those who wish to build he imagines to be those who have made up their minds to stay behind in Chaldea, and who, whilst their brethren who have returned to their native land are preparing to build a temple there, want to have one of their own, just as the Jews in Egypt built one for themselves in Leontopolis. Without some such supposition as this, Hitzig thinks it altogether impossible to discover the thread which connects the different vv. together. This view is at any rate better than that of Umbreit, who imagines that the prophet places us here “on the loftiest spiritual height of the Christian development.” “In the new Jerusalem,” he says, “there will be no temple seen, nor any sacrifice; Jehovah forbids these in the strongest terms, regarding them as equivalent to mortal sins.” But the prophet, if this were his meaning, would involve himself in self-contradiction, inasmuch as, according to <reference osisRef="Isa.56.1-Isa.56.12">Isa 56:1-12</reference> and 60, there will be a temple in the new Jerusalem with perpetual sacrifice, which this prophecy also presupposes in Isa 66:20. (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.66.6">Isa 66:6</reference>); and secondly, he would contradict other prophets, such as Ezekiel and Zechariah, and the spirit of the Old Testament generally, in which the statement, that whoever slaughters a sacrificial animal in the new Jerusalem will be as bad as a murderer, has no parallel, and is in fact absolutely impossible. According to Hitzig’s view, on the other hand, v. 3 <hi type="italic">a</hi> affirms, that the worship which they would be bound to perform in their projected temple would be an abomination to Jehovah, however thoroughly it might be made to conform to the Mosaic ritual. But there is nothing in the text to sustain the idea, that there is any intention here to condemn the building of a temple to Jehovah in Chaldaea, nor is such an explanation by any means necessary to make the text clear. The condemnation on the part of Jehovah has reference to the temple, which the returning exiles intend to build in Jerusalem. The prophecy is addressed to the entire body now ready to return, and says to the whole without exception, that Jehovah, the Creator of heaven and earth, does not stand in need of any house erected by human hands, and then proceeds to separate the penitent from those that are at enmity against God, rejects in the most scornful manner all offerings in the form of worship on the part of the latter, and threatens them with divine retribution, having dropped in <reference osisRef="Isa.66.3-Isa.66.4">Isa 66:3-4</reference> the form of address to the entire body. Just as in the Psalm of Asaph (Ps 50) Jehovah refuses animal and other material offerings as such, because the whole of the animal world, the earth and the fulness thereof, are His possession, so here He addresses this question to the entire body of the exiles: What kind of house is there that ye could build, that would be worthy of me, and what kind of place that would be worthy of being assigned to me as a resting-place? On <hi type="italic">mâqōm</hi> <hi type="italic">menūchâthı̄</hi>, <hi type="italic">locus qui sit requies mea</hi> (apposition instead of genitive connection). He needs no temple; for heaven is His throne, and the earth His footstool. He is the Being who filleth all, the Creator, and therefore the possessor, of the universe; and if men think to do Him a service by building Him a temple, and forget His infinite majesty in their concern for their own contemptible fabric, He wants to temple at all. “All these” refer, as if pointing with the finger, to the world of visible objects that surround us. ויּהיוּ (from היה, <hi type="italic">existere</hi>, <hi type="italic">fieri</hi>) is used in the same sense as the ויהי which followed the creative יהי. In this His exaltation He is not concerned about a temple; but His gracious look is fixed upon the man who is as follows (<hi type="italic">zeh</hi> pointing forwards as in <reference osisRef="Isa.58.6">Isa 58:6</reference>), viz., upon the mourner, the man of broken heart, who is filled with reverential awe at the word of His revelation. <div eID="gen13693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13694" type="x-p"/> We may see from <reference osisRef="Ps.51.9">Psa 51:9</reference> what the link of connection is between <reference osisRef="Isa.66.2">Isa 66:2</reference> and Isa 66:3. So far as the mass of the exiles were concerned, who had not been humbled by their sufferings, and whom the preaching of the prophet could not bring to reflection, He did not want any temple or sacrifice from them. The sacrificial acts, to which such detestable predicates are here applied, are such as end with the merely external act, whilst the inward feelings of the person presenting the sacrifice are altogether opposed to the idea of both the animal sacrifice and the meat-offering, more especially to that desire for salvation which was symbolized in all the sacrifices; in other words, they are sacrificial acts regarded as νεκρὰ ἔργα, the lifeless works of men spiritually dead. The articles of <hi type="italic">hasshōr</hi> and <hi type="italic">hasseh</hi> are used as generic with reference to sacrificial animals. The slaughter of an ox was like the slaying (<hi type="italic">makkēh</hi> construct with <hi type="italic">tzere</hi>) of a man (for the association of ideas, see <reference osisRef="Gen.49.6">Gen 49:6</reference>); the sacrifice (<hi type="italic">zōbhēăch</hi> like <hi type="italic">shâchat</hi> is sometimes applied to slaughtering for the purpose of eating; here, however, it refers to an animal prepared for Jehovah) of a sheep like the strangling of a dog, that unclean animal (for the association of ideas, see <reference osisRef="Job.30.1">Job 30:1</reference>); the offerer up (<hi type="italic">me‛ōlēh</hi>) of a meat-offering (like one who offered up) swine’s blood, i.e., as if he was offering up the blood of this most unclean animal upon the altar; he who offered incense as an <hi type="italic">'azkârâh</hi> (see at <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.1.13">Isa 1:13</reference></hi>) like one who blessed <hi type="italic">'âven</hi>, i.e., godlessness, used here as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.23">1Sa 15:23</reference>, and also in Hosea in the change of the name of Bethel into <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> <hi type="italic">'Aven</hi>, for idolatry, or rather in a concrete sense for the worthless idols themselves, all of which, according to <reference osisRef="Isa.41.29">Isa 41:29</reference>, are nothing but <hi type="italic">'âven</hi>. Rosenmüller, Gesenius, Hitzig, Stier, and even Jerome, have all correctly rendered it in this way, “as if he blessed an idol” (<hi type="italic">quasi qui benedicat idolo</hi>); and Vitringa, “<hi type="italic">cultum exhibens vano numini</hi>” (offering worship to a vain god). Such explanations as that of Luther, on the other hand, viz., “as if he praised that which was wrong,” are opposed to the antithesis, and also to the presumption of a concrete object to מברך (blessing); whilst that of Knobel, “praising vainly” (<hi type="italic">'âven</hi> being taken as an <hi type="italic">acc. Adv.</hi>), yields too tame an antithesis, and is at variance with the usage of the language. In this condemnation of the ritual acts of worship, the closing prophecy of the book of Isaiah coincides with the first (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.11-Isa.1.15">Isa 1:11-15</reference>). But that it is not sacrifices in themselves that are rejected, but the sacrifices of those whose hearts are divided between Jehovah and idols, and who refuse to offer to Him the sacrifice that is dearest to Him (<reference osisRef="Ps.51.19">Psa 51:19</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.50.23">Psa 50:23</reference>), is evident from the correlative double-sentence that follows in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.66.3">Isa 66:3</reference></hi> and <reference osisRef="Isa.66.4">Isa 66:4</reference>, which is divided into two masoretic verses, as the only means of securing symmetry. <hi type="italic">Gam</hi> ... <hi type="italic">gam</hi>, which means in other cases, “both ... and also,” or in negative sentences “neither ... nor,” means here, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.12">Jer 51:12</reference>, “as assuredly the one as the other,” in other words, “as ... so.” They have chosen their own ways, which are far away from those of Jehovah, and their soul has taken pleasure, not in the worship of Jehovah, but in all kinds of heathen abominations (<hi type="italic">shiqqūtsēhem</hi>, as in many other places, after <reference osisRef="Deut.29.16">Deu 29:16</reference>); therefore Jehovah wants no temple built by them or with their co-operation, nor any restoration of sacrificial worship at their hands. But according to the law of retribution, He chooses <hi type="italic">tha‛ălūlēhem</hi>, <hi type="italic">vexationes eorum</hi> (lxx τὰ ἐμπαίγματα αὐτῶν: see at <reference osisRef="Isa.3.4">Isa 3:4</reference>), with the suffix of the object: fates that will use them ill, and brings their terrors upon them, i.e., such a condition of life as will inspire them with terror (<hi type="italic">megūrōth</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.34.5">Psa 34:5</reference>).
entries.ee2a414a53d6356b35cbb3486e7cf0ea22f39101: <reference osisRef="Isa.66.5">Isa 66:5</reference> <div eID="gen13694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13695" type="x-p"/> From the heathenish majority, with their ungodly hearts, the prophet now turns to the minority, consisting of those who tremble with reverential awe when they hear the word of God. They are called to hear how Jehovah will accept them in defiance of their persecutors. <hi type="italic">“Hear ye the word of Jehovah, ye that tremble at His word: your brethren that hate you, that thrust you from them for my name’s sake, say, 'Let Jehovah get honour, that we may see your joy:' they will be put to shame.”</hi> They that hate them are their own brethren, and (what makes the sin still greater) the name of Jehovah is the reason why they are hated by them. According to the accents, indeed (מנדיכם <hi type="italic">rebia</hi>, סמי <hi type="italic">pashta</hi>), the meaning would be, “your brethren say ...  'for my name’s sake (i.e., for me = out of goodness and love to us) will Jehovah glorify Himself,' - then we shall see your joy, but - they will be put to shame.” Rashi and other Jewish expositors interpret it in this or some similar way; but Rosenmüller, Stier, and Hahn are the only modern Christian expositors, who have done so, following the precedent of earlier commentators, who regarded the accents as binding. Luther, however, very properly disregarded them. If סמי למען be taken in connection with יכבד, it gives only a forced sense, which disturbs the relation of all the clauses; whereas this is preserved in all respects in the most natural and connected manner if we combine שמי למען with מנדּיכם שׂנאיכם, as we must do, according to such parallels as Mat 24:9. נדּה from נר, to scare away or thrust away (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.3">Amo 6:3</reference>, with the object in the dative), corresponds to ἀφορίζειν in <reference osisRef="Luke.6.22">Luk 6:22</reference> (compare Joh 16:22, “to put out of the synagogue”). The practice of excommunication, or putting under the ban (<hi type="italic">niddūi</hi>), reaches beyond the period of the Herodians (see <hi type="italic">Eduyoth</hi> v. 6),<note placement="foot">Compare <hi type="italic">Wiesner: Der Bann in seiner gesch</hi>. <hi type="italic">Entwickelung auf dem Boden des Judenthums</hi>, 1864.</note> at any rate as far back as the times succeeding the captivity; but in the passage before us it is quite sufficient to understand <hi type="italic">niddâh</hi> in the sense of a defamatory renunciation of fellowship. To the accentuators this שמי למען מנדיכם appeared quite unintelligible. They never considered that it had a confessional sense here, which certainly does not occur anywhere else: viz., “for my name’s sake, which ye confess in word and deed.” With unbelieving scorn they say to those who confess Jehovah, and believe in the word of the true redemption: Let Jehovah glorify Himself (lit. let Him be, i.e., show Himself, glorious = <hi type="italic">yikkâbēd</hi>, cf., <reference osisRef="Job.14.21">Job 14:21</reference>), that we may thoroughly satisfy ourselves with looking at your joy. They regard their hope as deceptive, and the word of the prophet as fanaticism. These are they, who, when permission to return is suddenly given, will desire to accompany them, but will be disappointed, because they did not rejoice in faith before, and because, although they do now rejoice in that which is self-evident, they do this in a wrong way.
entries.113e2559065526be62034a94967b0b922f22947f: <reference osisRef="Isa.66.6">Isa 66:6</reference> <div eID="gen13695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13696" type="x-p"/> The city and temple, to which they desire to go, are nothing more, so far as they are concerned, than the places from which just judgment will issue. <hi type="italic">“Sound of tumult from the city! Sound from the Temple! Sound of Jehovah, who repays His enemies with punishment.”</hi> All three קול, to the second of which שׁאון must be supplied in thought, are in the form of interjectional exclamations (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.52.8">Isa 52:8</reference>). In the third, however, we have omitted the note of admiration, because here the interjectional clause approximates very nearly to a substantive clause (“it is the sound of Jehovah”), as the person shouting announces here who is the originator and cause of the noise which was so enigmatical at first. The city and temple are indeed still lying in ruins as the prophet is speaking; but even in this state they both preserve the holiness conferred upon them. They are the places where Jehovah will take up His abode once more; and even now, at the point at which promise and fulfilment coincide, they are in the very process of rising again. A loud noise (like the tumult of war) proceeds from it. It is Jehovah, He who is enthroned in Zion and rules from thence (<reference osisRef="Isa.31.9">Isa 31:9</reference>), who makes Himself heard in this loud noise (compare <reference osisRef="Joel.3.16">Joe 3:16</reference> with the derivative passage in <reference osisRef="Amos.1.2">Amo 1:2</reference>); it is He who awards punishment or reckons retribution to His foes. In other cases גּמוּל (השׁהיב) שׁלּם generally means to repay that which has been worked out (what has been deserved; e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.137.8">Psa 137:8</reference>, compare <reference osisRef="Isa.3.11">Isa 3:11</reference>); but in <reference osisRef="Isa.59.18">Isa 59:18</reference> <hi type="italic">gemūl</hi> was the parallel word to <hi type="italic">chēmâh</hi>, and therefore, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.35.4">Isa 35:4</reference>, it did not apply to the works of men, but to the retribution of the judge, just as in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.6">Jer 51:6</reference>, where it is used quite as absolutely. We have therefore rendered it “punishment;” “merited punishment” would express both sides of this double-sided word. By “His enemies,” according to the context, we are to understand primarily the mass of the exiles, who were so estranged from God, and yet withal so full of demands and expectations.
entries.3d9c17b5303f681c5e8ee2fd407fed91e26fb158: <reference osisRef="Isa.66.7-Isa.66.9">Isa 66:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen13696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13697" type="x-p"/> All of these fall victims to the judgment; and yet Zion is not left either childless or without population. <hi type="italic">“Before she travailed she brought forth; before pains came upon her, she was delivered of a boy. Who hath heard such a thing? Who hath seen anything like it? Are men delivered of a land in one day? or is a nation begotten at once? For Zion hath travailed, yea, hath brought forth her children. Should I bring to the birth, and not cause to bring forth? saith Jehovah: or should I, who cause to bring forth, shut it? saith thy God.”</hi> Before Zion travaileth, before any labour pains come upon her (<hi type="italic">chēbhel</hi> with <hi type="italic">tzere</hi>), she has already given birth, or brought with ease into the world a male child (<hi type="italic">hı̄mlit</hi> like <hi type="italic">millēt</hi>, in <reference osisRef="Isa.34.15">Isa 34:15</reference>, to cause to glide out). This boy, of whom she is delivered with such marvellous rapidity, is a whole land full of men, an entire nation. The seer exclaims with amazement, like Zion herself in <reference osisRef="Isa.49.21">Isa 49:21</reference>, “who hath heard such a thing, or seen anything like it? is a land brought to the birth (<hi type="italic">hăyūchal</hi> followed by <hi type="italic">'erets</hi> for <hi type="italic">hăthūchal</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.13.6">Gen 13:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.18">Isa 9:18</reference>; Ges. §147), i.e., the population of a whole land (as in Jdg 18:30), and that in one day, or a nation born all at once (<hi type="italic">yivvâlēd</hi>, with <hi type="italic">munach</hi> attached to the <hi type="italic">kametz</hi>, and <hi type="italic">metheg</hi> to the <hi type="italic">tzere</hi>)? This unheard-of event has taken place now, for Zion has travailed, yea, has also brought forth her children,” - not one child, but her children, a whole people that calls her mother.<note placement="foot">There is a certain similarity in the saying, with which a <hi type="italic">talmud</hi>ic teacher roused up the sleepy scholars of the Beth ha-Midrash: “There was once a woman, who was delivered of 600,000 children in one day,” viz., Jochebed, who, when she gave birth to Moses, brought 600,000 to the light of freedom (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.37">Exo 12:37</reference>).</note> “For” (<hi type="italic">kı̄</hi>) presupposes the suppressed thought, that this unexampled event has now occurred: <hi type="italic">yâledâh</hi> follows <hi type="italic">châlâh</hi> with <hi type="italic">gam</hi>, because <hi type="italic">chı̄l</hi> signifies strictly <hi type="italic">parturire</hi>; <hi type="italic">yâl</hi>, <hi type="italic">parere</hi>. Zion, the mother, is no other than the woman of the sun in Rev 12; ; but the child born of her there is the shepherd of the nations, who proceeds from her at the end of the days, whereas here it is the new Israel of the last days; for the church, which is saved through all her tribulations, is both the mother of the Lord, by whom Babel is overthrown, and the mother of that Israel which inherits the promises, that the unbelieving mass have failed to obtain. <reference osisRef="Isa.66.9">Isa 66:9</reference> follows with an emphatic confirmation of the things promised. Jehovah inquires: “Should I create the delivery (cause the child to break through the matrix) and not the birth (both <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi>, causative), so that although the child makes an effort to pass the opening of the womb, it never comes to the light of day? Or should I be one to bring it to the birth, and then to have closed, viz., the womb, so that the word of bringing forth should remain ineffectual, when all that is required is the last effort to bring to the light the fruit of the womb?” From the expression “thy God,” we see that the questions are addressed to Zion, whose faith they are intended to strengthen. According to Hofmann (<hi type="italic">Schriftbeweis</hi>, ii. 1, 149, 150), the future יאמר affirms what Jehovah will say, when the time for bringing forth arrives, and the perfect אמר what He is saying now: “Should I who create the bringing forth have shut up?” And He comforts the now barren daughter Zion (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.1">Isa 54:1</reference>) with the assurance, that her barrenness is not meant to continue for ever. “The prediction,” says Hofmann, “which is contained in ה יאמר, of the ultimate issue of the fate of Zion, is so far connected with the consolation administered for the time present, that she who is barren now is exhorted to anticipate the time when the former promise shall be fulfilled.” But this change in the standpoint is artificial, and contrary to the general use of the expression ה יאמר elsewhere (see at <reference osisRef="Isa.40.1">Isa 40:1</reference>). Moreover, the meaning of the two clauses, which constitute here as elsewhere a disjunctive double question in form more than in sense, really runs into one. The first member affirms that Jehovah will complete the bringing to the birth; the second, that He will not ultimately frustrate what He has almost brought to completion: <hi type="italic">an ego sum is qui parere faciat et</hi> (<hi type="italic">uterum</hi>) <hi type="italic">occluserim</hi> (<hi type="italic">occludam</hi>)? There is no other difference between יאמר and אמר, than that the former signifies the word of God which is sounding at the present moment, the latter the word that has been uttered and is resounding still. The prophetic announcement of our prophet has advanced so far, that the promised future is before the door. The church of the future is already like the fruit of the body ripe for the birth, and about to separate itself from the womb of Zion, which has been barren until now. The God by whom everything has been already so far prepared, will suddenly cause Zion to become a mother - a boy, viz., a whole people after Jehovah’s own heart, will suddenly lie in her lap, and this new-born Israel, not the corrupt mass, will build a temple for Jehovah.
entries.9fa160f2e318e9d2482a32ab891f09990cb25bac: <reference osisRef="Isa.66.10-Isa.66.11">Isa 66:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen13697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13698" type="x-p"/> In the anticipation of such a future, those who inwardly participate in the present sufferings of Zion are to rejoice beforehand in the change of all their suffering into glory. <hi type="italic">“Rejoice ye with Jerusalem, and exult over her, all ye that love her; be ye delightfully glad with her, all ye that mourn over her, that he may suck and be satisfied with the breast of her consolations, that ye may sip and delight yourselves in the abundance of her glory.”</hi> Those who love Jerusalem (the abode of the church, and the church itself), who mourn over her (<hi type="italic">hith'abbēl</hi>, inwardly mourn, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.35">1Sa 15:35</reference>, prove and show themselves to be mourners and go into mourning, <hi type="italic">b. Moëd katan</hi> 20 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, the word generally used in prose, whereas אבל, to be thrown into mourning, to mourn, only occurs in the higher style; compare ציּון אבלי, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.18">Isa 57:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.2-Isa.61.3">Isa 61:2-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.20">Isa 60:20</reference>), these are even now to rejoice in spirit with Jerusalem and exult on her account (<hi type="italic">bâh</hi>), and share her ecstatic delight with her (<hi type="italic">'ittâh</hi>), in order that when that in which they now rejoice in spirit shall be fulfilled, they may suck and be satisfied, etc. Jerusalem is regarded as a mother, and the rich actual consolation, which she receives (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.3">Isa 51:3</reference>), as the milk that enters her breasts (<hi type="italic">shōd</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Isa.60.16">Isa 60:16</reference>), and from which she now supplies her children with plentiful nourishment. זיז, which is parallel to שׁד (not זיו, a reading which none of the ancients adopted), signifies a moving, shaking abundance, which oscillates to and fro like a great mass of water, from זאזא, to move by fits and starts, for <hi type="italic">pellere movere</hi> is the radical meaning common in such combinations of letters as זא, זע, רא, <reference osisRef="Ps.42.5">Psa 42:5</reference>, to which Bernstein and Knobel have correctly traced the word; whereas the meaning <hi type="italic">emicans fluxus</hi> (Schröder), or <hi type="italic">radians copia</hi> (Kocher), to pour out in the form of rays, has nothing to sustain it in the usage of the language.
entries.1c266a6dbb01b92bb7fd25bf55c05a5916f67cff: <reference osisRef="Isa.66.12">Isa 66:12</reference> <div eID="gen13698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13699" type="x-p"/> The reason is now given, why the church of the future promises such abundant enjoyment to those who have suffered with her. <hi type="italic">“For thus saith Jehovah, Behold, I guide peace to her like a river, and the glory of the Gentiles like an overflowing stream, that ye may suck; ye shall be borne upon arms, and fondled upon knees.”</hi> Jehovah guides or turns (<reference osisRef="Gen.39.21">Gen 39:21</reference>) peace to Jerusalem, the greatest of all inward blessings, and at the same time the most glorious of all the outward blessings, that are in the possession of the Gentile world (<hi type="italic">kâbhōd</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Isa.56.6">Isa 56:6</reference>), both of them in the richest superabundance (“like a river,” as in <reference osisRef="Isa.48.18">Isa 48:18</reference>), so that (<hi type="italic">perf. cons.</hi>) “ye may be able to suck yourselves full according to your heart’s desire” (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.16">Isa 60:16</reference>). The figure of the new maternity of Zion, and of her children as <hi type="italic">quasimodogeniti</hi>, is still preserved. The members of the church can then revel in peace and wealth, like a child at its mother’s breasts. The world is now altogether in the possession of the church, because the church is altogether God's. The allusion to the heathen leads on to the thought, which was already expressed in a similar manner in <reference osisRef="Isa.49.22">Isa 49:22</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.60.4">Isa 60:4</reference> : “on the side (arm or shoulder) will ye be carried, and fondled (שׁעשׁע, <hi type="italic">pulpal</hi> of the <hi type="italic">pilpel</hi> שׁעשׁע, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.8">Isa 11:8</reference>) upon the knees,” viz., by the heathen, who will vie with one another in the effort to show you tenderness and care (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.23">Isa 49:23</reference>).
entries.5aef7bd1769d048c8e3a73f32d8d2583fdba3ec0: <reference osisRef="Isa.66.13">Isa 66:13</reference> <div eID="gen13699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13700" type="x-p"/> The prophet now looks upon the members of the church as having grown up, as it were, from childhood to maturity: they suck like a child, and are comforted like a grown-up son. <hi type="italic">“Like a man whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you, and ye shall be comforted in Jerusalem.”</hi> Hitzig says that <hi type="italic">'ı̄sh</hi> is not well chosen; but how easily could the prophet have written <hi type="italic">bēn</hi> (son), as in Isa 49:15! He writes <hi type="italic">'ı̄sh</hi>, however, not indeed in the unmeaning sense in which the lxx has taken it, viz., ὡς εἴ τινα μήτηρ παρακαλέσει, but looking upon the people, whom he had previously thought of as children, as standing before him as one man. Israel is now like a man who has escaped from bondage and returned home from a foreign land, full of mournful recollections, the echoing sounds of which entirely disappear in the maternal arms of divine love there in Jerusalem, the beloved home, which was the home of its thoughts even in the strange land.
entries.4b56a7444c9681c273554629b50d5b41e309cc24: <reference osisRef="Isa.66.14">Isa 66:14</reference> <div eID="gen13700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13701" type="x-p"/> Wherever they look, joy now meets their eye. <hi type="italic">“And ye will see, and your heart will be joyful, and your bones will flourish like young herbage; and thus does the hand of Jehovah make itself known in His servants, and fiercely does He treat His enemies.”</hi> They will see, and their heart will rejoice, i.e., (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">Isa 53:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.5">Isa 60:5</reference>) they will enjoy a heart-cheering prospect, and revive again with such smiling scenery all around. The body is like a tree The bones are its branches. These will move and extend themselves in the fulness of rejuvenated strength (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.58.11">Isa 58:11</reference>, <hi type="italic">et ossa tua expedita faciet</hi>); and thus will the hand of Jehovah practically become known (<hi type="italic">venwde‛âh</hi>, <hi type="italic">perf. cons.</hi>) in His servants - that hand under whose gracious touch all vernal life awakens, whether in body or in mind. And thus is it with the surviving remnant of Israel, whereas Jehovah is fiercely angry with His foes. The first את is used in a prepositional sense, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.67.2">Psa 67:2</reference>, viz., “in His servants, so that they come to be acquainted with it”; the second in an accusative sense, for <hi type="italic">zâ'am</hi> is either connected with על, or as in Zec 1:12; Mal 1:4, with the accusative of the object. It is quite contrary to the usage of the language to take both את according to the phrase (עס) את (רעה) מובה עשׂה.
entries.89bcb0e21e37664a5a085ea9e4143c70069e48a9: <reference osisRef="Isa.66.15">Isa 66:15</reference> <div eID="gen13701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13702" type="x-p"/> The prophecy now takes a new turn with the thought expressed in the words, “and fiercely does He treat His enemies.” The judgment of wrath, which prepares the way for the redemption and ensures its continuance, is described more minutely in <reference osisRef="Isa.66.15">Isa 66:15</reference> : <hi type="italic">“For behold Jehovah, in the fire will He come, and His chariots are like the whirlwind, to pay out His wrath in burning heat, and His threatening passeth into flames of fire.”</hi> Jehovah comes <hi type="italic">bâ'ēsh</hi>, <hi type="italic">in igne</hi> (Jerome; the lxx, on the contrary, render it arbitrarily ὡς πῦρ <hi type="italic">kâ'ēsh</hi>), since it is the fiery side of His glory, in which He appears, and fire pours from Him, which is primarily the intense excitement of the powers of destruction within God Himself (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.17">Isa 10:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.27">Isa 30:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.9">Psa 18:9</reference>), and in these is transformed into cosmical powers of destruction (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.6">Isa 29:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.30">Isa 30:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.13">Psa 18:13</reference>). He is compared to a warrior, driving along upon war-chariots resembling stormy wind, which force everything out of their way, and crush to pieces whatever comes under their wheels. The plural מרכּבתיו (His chariots) is probably not merely amplifying, but a strict plural; for Jehovah, the One, can manifest Himself in love or wrath in different places at the same time. The very same substantive clause מרכבתיו וכסופה occurs in <reference osisRef="Jer.4.13">Jer 4:13</reference>, where it is not used of Jehovah, however, but of the Chaldeans. Observe also that Jeremiah there proceeds immediately with a derivative passage from Hab 1:8. In the following clause denoting the object, אפּו בּחמה להשׁיב, we must not adopt the rendering, “to breathe out His wrath in burning heat” (Hitzig), for <hi type="italic">hēshı̄bh</hi> may mean <hi type="italic">respirare</hi>, but not <hi type="italic">exspirare</hi> (if this were the meaning, it would be better to read להשּׁיב from נשׁב, as Lowth does); nor “<hi type="italic">ut iram suam furore sedet</hi>” (Meier), for even in <reference osisRef="Job.9.13">Job 9:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.38">Psa 78:38</reference>, עפו השיב does not mean to still or cool His wrath, but to turn it away or take it back; not even “to direct His wrath in burning heat” (Ges., Kn.), for in this sense <hi type="italic">hēshı̄bh</hi> would be connected with an object with ל, אל (<reference osisRef="Job.15.13">Job 15:13</reference>), על (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.25">Isa 1:25</reference>). It has rather the meaning <hi type="italic">reddere</hi> in the sense of <hi type="italic">retribuere</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">athâba</hi>, syn. <hi type="italic">shillēm</hi>), and “to pay back, or pay out, His wrath” is equivalent to <hi type="italic">hēshı̄bh</hi> <hi type="italic">nâqâm</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.41">Deu 32:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.43">Deu 32:43</reference>), Hence עפו בחמה does not stand in a permutative relation instead of a genitive one (viz., <hi type="italic">in fervore</hi>, <hi type="italic">riâ</hi> <hi type="italic">suâ</hi> = <hi type="italic">irae suae</hi>), but is an adverbial definition, just as in Isa 42:25. That the payment of the wrath deserved takes place in burning heat, and His rebuke (<hi type="italic">ge‛ârâh</hi>) in flames of fire, are thoughts that answer to one another.
entries.64ea2b03e03836f50dc138ec894675ca3f22dd7d: <reference osisRef="Isa.66.16">Isa 66:16</reference> <div eID="gen13702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13703" type="x-p"/> Jehovah appears with these warlike terrors because He is coming for a great judgment. <hi type="italic">“For in the midst of fire Jehovah holds judgment, and in the midst of His sword with all flesh; and great will be the multitude of those pierced through by Jehovah.”</hi> The fire, which is here introduced as the medium of judgment, points to destructive occurrences of nature, and the sword to destructive occurrences of history. At the same time all the emphasis is laid here, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.34.5-Isa.34.6">Isa 34:5-6</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Isa 27:1</reference>), upon the direct action of Jehovah Himself. The parallelism in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.66.16">Isa 66:16</reference></hi> is progressive. <hi type="italic">Nishpat</hi> <hi type="italic">'ēth</hi>, “to go into judgment with a person,” as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.22">Eze 38:22</reference> (cf., עם in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.14">Isa 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joel.3.2">Joe 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.22.8">2Ch 22:8</reference>; μετά, <reference osisRef="Luke.11.31-Luke.11.32">Luk 11:31-32</reference>). We find a resemblance to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.66.16">Isa 66:16</reference></hi> in Zep 2:12, and this is not the only resemblance to our prophecy in that strongly reproductive prophet.
entries.7ab32758accf3a8e632d7c14eb8ef86dcbb019b6: <reference osisRef="Isa.66.17">Isa 66:17</reference> <div eID="gen13703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13704" type="x-p"/> The judgment predicted here is a judgment upon nations, and falls not only upon the heathen, but upon the great mass of Israel, who have fallen away from their election of grace and become like the heathen. <hi type="italic">“They that consecrate themselves and purify themselves for the gardens behind one in the midst, who eat swine’s flesh and abomination and the field-mouse-they will come to an end together, saith Jehovah.”</hi> The persons are first of all described; and then follows the judgment pronounced, as the predicate of the sentence. They subject themselves to the heathen rites of lustration, and that with truly bigoted thoroughness, as is clearly implied by the combination of the two synonyms <hi type="italic">hammithqaddeshı̄m</hi> and <hi type="italic">hammittahărı̄m</hi> (<hi type="italic">hithpael</hi> with an assimilated <hi type="italic">tav</hi>), which, like the Arabic <hi type="italic">qadusa</hi> and <hi type="italic">tahura</hi>, are both traceable to the radical idea ἀφορίζειν. The אל of תונּגּה־לא is to be understood as relating to the object or behoof: their intention being directed to the gardens as places of worship (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.29">Isa 1:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.3">Isa 65:3</reference>), <hi type="italic">ad sacra in lucis obeunda</hi>, as Shelling correctly explains. In the <hi type="italic">chethib</hi> בּתּוך אחד אחר, the אחד (for which we may also read אחד, the form of connection, although the two <hi type="italic">pathachs</hi> of the text belong to the <hi type="italic">keri</hi>) is in all probability the hierophant, who leads the people in the performances of the rites of religious worship and as he is represented as standing in the midst (בּתּוך) of the worshipping crowd that surrounds him, <hi type="italic">'achar</hi> (behind, after) cannot be understood locally, as if they formed his train or tail, but temporally or in the way of imitation. He who stands in their midst performs the ceremonies before them, and they follow him, i.e., perform them <hi type="italic">after</hi> him. This explanation leaves nothing to be desired. The <hi type="italic">keri</hi>, <hi type="italic">'achath</hi>, is based upon the assumption that <hi type="italic">'achad</hi> must refer to the idol, and substitutes therefore the feminine, no doubt with an allusion to <hi type="italic">'ăshērâh</hi>, so that <hi type="italic">battâvekh</hi> (in the midst) is to be taken as referring not to the midst of the worshipping congregation, but to the midst of the gardens. This would be quite as suitable; for even if it were not expressly stated, we should have to assume that the sacred tree of Astarte, or her statue, occupied the post of honour in the midst of the garden, and <hi type="italic">'achar</hi> would correspond to the phrase in the Pentateuch, אחרים אלהים אחרי זנה. But the foregoing expression, <hi type="italic">sanctificantes et mundantes se</hi> (consecrating and purifying), does not favour this sense of the word <hi type="italic">'achar</hi> (why not ל = לכבוד?), nor do we see why the name of the goddess should be suppressed, or why she should be simply hinted at in the word אחת (one). אחד (אחד) has its sufficient explanation in the antithesis between the one choir-leader and the many followers; but if we take <hi type="italic">'achath</hi> as referring to the goddess, we can find no intelligible reason or object. <div eID="gen13704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13705" type="x-p"/> Some again have taken both <hi type="italic">'achad</hi> and <hi type="italic">'achath</hi> to be the proper name of the idol.
